import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Orchard-planting problem

The orchard-planting problem asks for the maximum number $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ of
$3$-point lines (lines containing exactly three of the points) attainable by a configuration of
$n$ points in the plane.

Burr, Grünbaum and Sloane (1974) constructed, for every $n \geq 3$, $n$ points with
$\lfloor n(n-3)/6 \rfloor + 1$ three-point lines. Green and Tao (2013) proved that this is the
maximum for all sufficiently large $n$. The exact value of $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ for every
$n$ remains open: the threshold in the Green–Tao theorem is not explicit, and the formula fails
for some small $n$ (for $n = 7$ the triangle, its three midpoints and its centroid give $6$
three-point lines while the formula gives $5$).

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Orchard-planting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard-planting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in
  mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- S. A. Burr, B. Grünbaum, N. J. A. Sloane, *The orchard problem*, Geometriae Dedicata 2 (1974),
  397–424. [doi:10.1007/BF00147569](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00147569)
- B. Green, T. Tao, *On sets defining few ordinary lines*, Discrete Comput. Geom. 50 (2013),
  409–468. [arXiv:1208.4714](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4714)
- [OEIS A003035](https://oeis.org/A003035)
-/

namespace OrchardPlantingProblem

open EuclideanGeometry Filter

/-- `kPointLines k P` is the set of lines of the plane that contain exactly `k` points of the
finite point set `P`. A line is represented by the affine span of two distinct points of `P`, so
that only lines determined by `P` are counted. -/
def kPointLines (k : ℕ) (P : Finset ℝ²) : Set (AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²) :=
  {L | (∃ p ∈ P, ∃ q ∈ P, p ≠ q ∧ L = line[ℝ, p, q]) ∧
    ((L : Set ℝ²) ∩ P).ncard = k}

/-- `maxThreePointLines n` is $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$, the maximum number of $3$-point lines
attainable by a configuration of `n` points in the plane. The set of attainable values is
nonempty and bounded above by $\lfloor n(n-1)/6 \rfloor$, since two distinct lines share at most
one point, so the supremum is a maximum. For `n < 3` the value is `0`. -/
noncomputable def maxThreePointLines (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {(kPointLines 3 P).ncard | (P : Finset ℝ²) (_ : P.card = n)}

/-- **Orchard-planting problem.** Determine, for every $n$, the maximum number
$t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ of $3$-point lines attainable by a configuration of $n$ points in the
plane. The candidate formula $\lfloor n(n-3)/6 \rfloor + 1$ is only known to be correct for all
sufficiently large $n$ (Green–Tao) and fails for some small $n$, for example $n = 7$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 5 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem : maxThreePointLines = answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/-- **Orchard-planting problem for large $n$** (Green–Tao 2013, with the lower bound of
Burr–Grünbaum–Sloane 1974). There is an $n_0$ such that for all $n \geq n_0$, the maximum
number of $3$-point lines attainable by a configuration of $n$ points in the plane is exactly
$$t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n) = \left\lfloor \frac{n(n-3)}{6} \right\rfloor + 1.$$
Green and Tao prove the upper bound for all point sets of sufficient size; the matching lower
bound is the Burr–Grünbaum–Sloane construction, valid for every $n \geq 3$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem.variants.eventually :
    ∀ᶠ n in atTop, maxThreePointLines n = n * (n - 3) / 6 + 1 := by
  sorry

/-- **Green–Tao upper bound** (2013). For all point sets of sufficient size, $n \geq n_0$, a
configuration of $n$ points in the plane determines at most
$\lfloor n(n-3)/6 \rfloor + 1$ lines containing exactly three of the points. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem.variants.green_tao_upper_bound :
    ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ P : Finset ℝ², P.card = n →
      (kPointLines 3 P).ncard ≤ n * (n - 3) / 6 + 1 := by
  sorry

/-- **Burr–Grünbaum–Sloane lower bound** (1974). For every $n \geq 3$ there is a configuration
of $n$ points in the plane with at least $\lfloor n(n-3)/6 \rfloor + 1$ lines containing exactly
three of the points. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem.variants.bgs_lower_bound (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) :
    ∃ P : Finset ℝ², P.card = n ∧ n * (n - 3) / 6 + 1 ≤ (kPointLines 3 P).ncard := by
  sorry

/-- Fewer than three points determine no $3$-point line. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 52]
theorem maxThreePointLines_zero : maxThreePointLines 0 = 0 := by
  have h : ∀ P : Finset ℝ², P.card = 0 → (kPointLines 3 P).ncard = 0 := by
    intro P hP
    rw [Finset.card_eq_zero] at hP
    subst hP
    simp [kPointLines]
  have : {(kPointLines 3 P).ncard | (P : Finset ℝ²) (_ : P.card = 0)} = {0} := by
    ext x
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨P, hP, rfl⟩
      exact h P hP
    · rintro rfl
      exact ⟨∅, Finset.card_empty, h ∅ Finset.card_empty⟩
  rw [maxThreePointLines, this, csSup_singleton]

end OrchardPlantingProblem

open EuclideanGeometry

namespace OrchardPlantingProblem

/--
The orchard number $t_3^{\mathrm{orchard}}(n)$ is the maximum, over all configurations of
$n$ distinct points in the real plane, of the number of affine lines containing exactly three
points of the configuration. The supremum is over a bounded set of natural numbers, so it is a
maximum. In particular, the value is zero when $n<3$.
-/
noncomputable def t₃ (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {m : ℕ | ∃ P : Finset ℝ², P.card = n ∧
    m = {L : AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ² |
      Module.finrank ℝ L.direction = 1 ∧ ((P : Set ℝ²) ∩ (L : Set ℝ²)).ncard = 3}.ncard}

/--
Determine, for every natural number $n$, the maximum number
$t_3^{\mathrm{orchard}}(n)$ of lines containing exactly three points that is attainable by a
configuration of $n$ points in the real plane. The requested answer is the entire sequence,
including its small values; no particular closed formula is asserted.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem :
    t₃ = answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
There is an absolute threshold such that, for every sufficiently large number $n$ of points, the
maximum number of lines containing exactly three points is
$\lfloor n(n-3)/6\rfloor+1$. Equivalently,
$t_3^{\mathrm{orchard}}(n)=n(n-3)/6+1$ eventually as $n$ tends to infinity.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem.variants.eventually :
    ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop, t₃ n = n * (n - 3) / 6 + 1 := by
  sorry

end OrchardPlantingProblem
modeling_decisions: Configurations are represented by `Finset ℝ²`, so their points are distinct and lie in the real affine plane used by the Wikipedia statement.

A geometric line is represented by an `AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²` whose direction has `Module.finrank` one. A line is counted only when its intersection with the configuration has `Set.ncard = 3`, excluding lines containing four or more selected points.

The orchard number is the `sSup` in `ℕ` of all line counts attained by configurations of cardinality `n`. These counts are bounded by the number of pairs of points, and the set of configurations is nonempty for every `n`; hence this models the attained maximum and gives zero for `n < 3`.

The open determination is represented by equality of the whole function `t₃ : ℕ → ℕ` with a function-valued `answer(sorry)`. This asks for all values without incorrectly asserting the Green–Tao formula at the known small exceptions.

The solved sufficient-size variant is stated with `∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop`. Its right-hand side uses natural subtraction and division; eventually `n ≥ 3`, so `n * (n - 3) / 6` is exactly `⌊n(n-3)/6⌋`.

The source says points in the plane, so the primary definition is affine rather than projective. For finite real configurations this is consistent with the affine formulation in the reference article.

/-!
# Orchard-planting problem

The orchard-planting problem asks for the largest possible number of lines containing exactly
three points of a configuration of a prescribed number of points in the real plane.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Orchard-planting problem*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard-planting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)

namespace OrchardPlantingProblem

/-- The number of lines containing exactly three points of a finite configuration `P` in the
real plane. Such a line is represented by its unique three-element subset `L` of `P`. The last
condition says that no other point of `P` lies on that line. -/
noncomputable def threePointLineCount (P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ)) : ℕ := by
  classical
  exact ((P.powersetCard 3).filter fun (L : Finset (ℝ × ℝ)) ↦
    Collinear ℝ (L : Set (ℝ × ℝ)) ∧
      ∀ p ∈ P, p ∉ L → ¬Collinear ℝ (insert p (L : Set (ℝ × ℝ)))).card

/-- `orchardNumber n` is the maximum number of lines containing exactly three configured points,
over all configurations of `n` distinct points in the real plane. -/
noncomputable def orchardNumber (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {m : ℕ | ∃ P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), P.card = n ∧ threePointLineCount P = m}

/--
**Orchard-planting problem.** Determine, for every natural number $n$, the maximum
$t_3^{\mathrm{orchard}}(n)$ of the number of lines containing exactly three points among $n$
distinct points in the real plane. In particular, this asks for the complete function, including
its exceptional small values, rather than asserting the eventual formula for every $n$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem :
    let solution : ℕ → ℕ := answer(sorry)
    ∀ n, orchardNumber n = solution n := by
  sorry

/--
Green and Tao's eventual solution of the orchard-planting problem, together with the matching
Burr--Grünbaum--Sloane construction: for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$t_3^{\mathrm{orchard}}(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{n(n-3)}6\right\rfloor+1.$$
The threshold is existential and is not made explicit.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem.variants.eventually :
    ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop, orchardNumber n = n * (n - 3) / 6 + 1 := by
  sorry

end OrchardPlantingProblem
modeling_decisions: A point configuration is a `Finset (ℝ × ℝ)`, so its points are distinct and lie in the real affine plane.

A line containing exactly three configured points is represented by its unique three-element subset `L`: `L` is collinear, and adjoining any configured point outside `L` makes the set non-collinear. This counts each geometric line once without introducing a quotient or chosen line equation.

The extremal function is the `sSup` in `ℕ` of attainable counts. The set is nonempty and bounded by the number of three-element subsets, so this supremum is the intended attained maximum; it also gives zero for `n < 3`.

The open slot is modeled as determination of the complete function via a function-valued `answer(sorry)`, with `∀ n` scoped after the answer. It deliberately does not assert the eventual Green–Tao formula for all natural numbers because of exceptional small values.

The solved variant uses `∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop` for an existential, non-explicit threshold. Natural-number division encodes the floor in `⌊n(n-3)/6⌋ + 1`; truncated natural subtraction is irrelevant on the eventual domain.
The eventual equality combines Green–Tao's sufficiently-large upper bound with the matching Burr–Grünbaum–Sloane construction, rather than recording only the upper inequality.

namespace OrchardPlantingProblem

/--
The number of lines in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ containing exactly `k` points of the finite
point set `P` (the *`k`-point lines*, or *`k`-rich lines*, of `P`). A line is an affine
subspace of `ℝ²` whose direction is one-dimensional.

For `k ≥ 2` there are only finitely many such lines (each is spanned by two points of `P`).
The problem below only uses `k = 3`.
-/
noncomputable def numRichLines (k : ℕ) (P : Finset ℝ²) : ℕ :=
  {L : AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ² |
    Module.finrank ℝ L.direction = 1 ∧ ((P : Set ℝ²) ∩ L).ncard = k}.ncard

/-- The empty configuration has no `k`-point lines for `k ≠ 0`. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]

The orchard-planting problem asks for the greatest possible number of lines containing exactly
three points of a configuration of a prescribed number of points in the real plane.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Orchard-planting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard-planting_problem)
- [BGS74] S. A. Burr, B. Grünbaum and N. J. A. Sloane, *The orchard problem*, Geometriae

- [GT13] B. Green and T. Tao, *On sets defining few ordinary lines*, Discrete Comput. Geom. 50

-/

namespace OrchardPlantingProblem

open scoped Classical in
/-- The number of lines containing exactly three points of a finite configuration `P` in the
real plane. Such a line is represented by its three-point intersection `L` with `P`. The last
condition says that no further point of `P` lies on the line through `L`. -/
noncomputable def threePointLineCount (P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ)) : ℕ :=
  (P.powerset.filter fun (L : Finset (ℝ × ℝ)) ↦
    L.card = 3 ∧ Collinear ℝ (L : Set (ℝ × ℝ)) ∧
      ∀ p ∈ P, Collinear ℝ (insert p (L : Set (ℝ × ℝ))) → p ∈ L).card

/-- `orchardNumber n` is the maximum number of lines containing exactly three points among all
configurations of `n` points in the real plane. It is zero when `n < 3`. -/
noncomputable def orchardNumber (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {k : ℕ | ∃ P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), P.card = n ∧ threePointLineCount P = k}

/-- **Orchard-planting problem.** Determine, for every natural number `n`, the maximum number
`orchardNumber n` of lines containing exactly three points of an `n`-point configuration in the
real plane. The unknown answer is allowed to depend on `n`; in particular, this does not assert
the eventual Green–Tao formula for the exceptional small values. -/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem :
    ∀ n : ℕ, orchardNumber n = answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/-- **Green–Tao theorem (with the Burr–Grünbaum–Sloane construction).** For all sufficiently
large `n`, the maximum number of lines containing exactly three points of an `n`-point
configuration in the real plane is
$\left\lfloor n(n-3)/6\right\rfloor+1$. Here natural-number division by `6` expresses the floor;
the eventual quantifier avoids the small values where this formula can fail. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem orchard_planting_problem.variants.eventually :
    ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop, orchardNumber n = n * (n - 3) / 6 + 1 := by
  sorry

end OrchardPlantingProblem

# Orchard-planting problem

The orchard-planting problem asks for the maximum number $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ of
$3$-point lines (lines containing exactly three of the points) attainable by a configuration
of $n$ points in the plane.

Burr, Grünbaum and Sloane [BGS74] constructed, for every $n \geq 3$, configurations of $n$
points with $\lfloor n(n-3)/6 \rfloor + 1$ three-point lines. Green and Tao [GT13] proved that
for all sufficiently large $n$ no configuration of $n$ points has more than this many
three-point lines, so $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n) = \lfloor n(n-3)/6 \rfloor + 1$ for all
sufficiently large $n$. The exact value for every $n$ is not known: the formula fails for some
small $n$ (for example $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(7) = 6$), and the threshold in the Green–Tao
theorem is not explicit.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard-planting_problem)
- [BGS74] Burr, S. A., Grünbaum, B., Sloane, N. J. A., *The orchard problem*.
  Geometriae Dedicata 2 (1974), 397–424.
- [GT13] Green, B., Tao, T., *On sets defining few ordinary lines*.
  Discrete Comput. Geom. 50 (2013), 409–468. [arXiv:1208.4714](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4714)
- [A003035](https://oeis.org/A003035)
-/

open EuclideanGeometry Filter

namespace OrchardPlantingProblem

/-- A line in the plane: an affine subspace whose direction is one-dimensional. -/
def IsLine (L : AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²) : Prop :=
  Module.finrank ℝ L.direction = 1

/-- The number of lines in the plane that contain exactly `k` points of the finite set `P`. -/
noncomputable def kPointLines (P : Finset ℝ²) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  {L : AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ² | IsLine L ∧ ((P : Set ℝ²) ∩ L).ncard = k}.ncard

/--
$t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$: the maximum number of $3$-point lines attainable by a configuration
of $n$ points in the plane. Two distinct points lie on exactly one line, so this number is at
most $\binom{n}{2} / 3$ and the supremum is attained.
-/
noncomputable def orchardNumber (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {kPointLines P 3 | (P : Finset ℝ²) (_ : P.card = n)}

/-- The line through two distinct points is a line. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]
theorem isLine_affineSpan_pair {a b : ℝ²} (h : a ≠ b) : IsLine line[ℝ, a, b] := by
  rw [IsLine, direction_affineSpan, vectorSpan_pair]
  exact finrank_span_singleton (vsub_ne_zero.mpr h)

/-- A line through two distinct points `a` and `b` is the line `line[ℝ, a, b]`. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]
theorem IsLine.eq_affineSpan_pair {L : AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²} (hL : IsLine L) {a b : ℝ²}
    (hab : a ≠ b) (ha : a ∈ L) (hb : b ∈ L) : L = line[ℝ, a, b] := by
  refine (AffineSubspace.eq_of_direction_eq_of_nonempty_of_le ?_ ⟨a, left_mem_affineSpan_pair ..⟩
    (affineSpan_pair_le_of_mem_of_mem ha hb)).symm
  exact Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq
    (AffineSubspace.direction_le (affineSpan_pair_le_of_mem_of_mem ha hb))
    ((isLine_affineSpan_pair hab).trans hL.symm)

/-- A line containing three points of the three-point set `{a, b, c}` is the line
`line[ℝ, a, b]`. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]
theorem IsLine.eq_affineSpan_pair_of_ncard_inter {L : AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²} (hL : IsLine L)
    {a b c : ℝ²} (hab : a ≠ b) (hac : a ≠ c) (hbc : b ≠ c)
    (h : ((({a, b, c} : Finset ℝ²) : Set ℝ²) ∩ L).ncard = 3) : L = line[ℝ, a, b] := by
  have hP : (({a, b, c} : Finset ℝ²) : Set ℝ²).ncard = 3 := by
    rw [Set.ncard_coe_finset, Finset.card_eq_three]
    exact ⟨a, b, c, hab, hac, hbc, rfl⟩
  have h := Set.inter_eq_left.mp (Set.eq_of_subset_of_ncard_le Set.inter_subset_left
    (hP.trans h.symm).le)
  simp only [Finset.coe_insert, Finset.coe_singleton, Set.insert_subset_iff,
    Set.singleton_subset_iff, SetLike.mem_coe] at h
  exact hL.eq_affineSpan_pair hab h.1 h.2.1

/-- A set of fewer than `k` points determines no `k`-point line. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]
theorem kPointLines_eq_zero_of_card_lt {P : Finset ℝ²} {k : ℕ} (h : P.card < k) :
    kPointLines P k = 0 := by
  unfold kPointLines
  convert Set.ncard_empty (AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²)
  ext L
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_empty_iff_false, iff_false, not_and]
  intro _ hL
  have := (Set.ncard_le_ncard (Set.inter_subset_left (s := (P : Set ℝ²)) (t := (L : Set ℝ²)))
    (Finset.finite_toSet P)).trans_lt (by simpa using h)
  omega

/-- Three distinct collinear points determine exactly one $3$-point line. -/
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem kPointLines_three {a b c : ℝ²} (hab : a ≠ b) (hac : a ≠ c) (hbc : b ≠ c)
    (hc : c ∈ line[ℝ, a, b]) : kPointLines {a, b, c} 3 = 1 := by
  rw [kPointLines, Set.ncard_eq_one]
  refine ⟨line[ℝ, a, b], Set.eq_singleton_iff_unique_mem.mpr ⟨⟨isLine_affineSpan_pair hab, ?_⟩,
    fun L ⟨hL, hL3⟩ => hL.eq_affineSpan_pair_of_ncard_inter hab hac hbc hL3⟩⟩
  rw [Set.inter_eq_left.mpr, Set.ncard_coe_finset, Finset.card_eq_three]
  · exact ⟨a, b, c, hab, hac, hbc, rfl⟩
  simp only [Finset.coe_insert, Finset.coe_singleton, Set.insert_subset_iff,
    Set.singleton_subset_iff, SetLike.mem_coe]
  exact ⟨left_mem_affineSpan_pair .., right_mem_affineSpan_pair .., hc⟩

/-- Three points determine at most one $3$-point line. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]
theorem kPointLines_le_one_of_card_eq_three {P : Finset ℝ²} (hP : P.card = 3) :
    kPointLines P 3 ≤ 1 := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, c, hab, hac, hbc, rfl⟩ := Finset.card_eq_three.mp hP
  unfold kPointLines
  refine (Set.ncard_le_ncard (t := {line[ℝ, a, b]}) ?_).trans_eq (Set.ncard_singleton _)
  rintro L ⟨hL, hL3⟩
  exact hL.eq_affineSpan_pair_of_ncard_inter hab hac hbc hL3

/-- Fewer than three points determine no $3$-point line. -/

theorem orchardNumber_eq_zero_of_lt_three {n : ℕ} (hn : n < 3) : orchardNumber n = 0 := by
  unfold orchardNumber
  convert csSup_singleton 0
  ext m
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨P, hP, rfl⟩
    exact kPointLines_eq_zero_of_card_lt (hP ▸ hn)
  · rintro rfl
    have hcard : ((Finset.range n).image
        fun i : ℕ => (EuclideanSpace.single (0 : Fin 2) (i : ℝ) : ℝ²)).card = n := by
      rw [Finset.card_image_of_injective _ fun i j hij => ?_, Finset.card_range]
      simpa using congrArg (fun v : ℝ² => v 0) hij
    exact ⟨_, hcard, kPointLines_eq_zero_of_card_lt (hcard.trans_lt hn)⟩

# Orchard-planting problem

The orchard-planting problem asks for the maximum number $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ of
$3$-point lines (lines containing exactly three of the points) attainable by a configuration
of $n$ points in the plane.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard-planting_problem)
- [BGS74] Burr, S. A., Grünbaum, B., Sloane, N. J. A., *The orchard problem*.

-/

open Filter
open scoped EuclideanGeometry

namespace OrchardPlantingProblem

/--
The set of lines in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ containing exactly $k$ points of the finite set
`P`. A line is recorded as the affine span of two distinct points of `P` lying on it, so for
$k \geq 2$ this is exactly the set of lines meeting `P` in precisely $k$ points.
-/
noncomputable def pointLines (k : ℕ) (P : Finset ℝ²) : Set (AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²) :=
  {L | ∃ p ∈ P, ∃ q ∈ P, p ≠ q ∧ L = line[ℝ, p, q] ∧ ((L : Set ℝ²) ∩ P).ncard = k}

/--
$t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$: the maximum number of $3$-point lines attainable by a configuration
of $n$ points in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$.

The number of $3$-point lines of an $n$-point set is at most $\binom{n}{2}/3$, so the
supremum is a maximum. For $n < 3$ the value is $0$.
-/
noncomputable def orchardNumber (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {(pointLines 3 P).ncard | (P : Finset ℝ²) (_ : P.card = n)}

/-- The empty configuration determines no $3$-point lines. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 52]
theorem orchardNumber_zero : orchardNumber 0 = 0 := by
  have : {(pointLines 3 P).ncard | (P : Finset ℝ²) (_ : P.card = 0)} = {0} := by
    ext x
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_singleton_iff, Finset.card_eq_zero]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨P, rfl, rfl⟩
      simp [pointLines]
    · rintro rfl
      exact ⟨∅, rfl, by simp [pointLines]⟩
  rw [orchardNumber, this, csSup_singleton]

/--
**Orchard-planting problem.** Determine, for every $n$, the maximum number
$t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ of $3$-point lines attainable by a configuration of $n$ points in the
plane (OEIS A003035).

Burr, Grünbaum and Sloane [BGS74] constructed $n$-point sets with
$\lfloor n(n-3)/6 \rfloor + 1$ three-point lines for every $n \geq 3$, and Green and Tao [GT13]
proved that this is the exact value of $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ for all sufficiently large
$n$ (see `orchard_planting_problem.variants.eventually`). The formula is not the answer for
every $n$: for instance $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(7) = 6$ while $\lfloor 7 \cdot 4/6 \rfloor + 1 = 5$,
and the threshold in the Green–Tao theorem is not explicit. The exact value of
$t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ for every $n$ is unknown.

  sorry
